title: Maryland board moves to set ceiling on what state will pay for Jardiance, Farxiga
summary: The Prescription Drug Affordability Board on Monday added Trulicity and Ozempic to the list of prescription drugs that are likely unaffordable for Marylanders. It also moved to cap payments on the first two drugs on the list, Jardiance and Farxiga.
content:
by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters November 17, 2025

by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters November 17, 2025

The Prescription Drug Affordability Board determined Monday that name-brand drugs Trulicity and Ozempic are likely unaffordable for Marylanders, adding them to two other drugs being considered for price caps by the state.

The board Monday also took steps toward finally approving caps on what the state would pay for those first two prescription drugs, Jardiance and Farxiga. The price caps have been years in the making, and may not be finalized for months yet, but advocates hailed Monday’s actions.

“It’s a major step forward in making high-cost drugs more affordable for state and local governments,” said Vinny DeMarco, a longtime supporter of the board’s effort and president of the Maryland Health Care for All Coalition. “It’s very important that this happens as soon as possible to start the clock ticking on when they can make high-cost drugs more affordable for everybody.”

The board ordered staff to draw up language to set a limit on how much state and local governments are willing to pay for Farxiga, a brand name for the drug dapagliflozin, and Jardiance, a brand name for empagliflozin, both of which are used in the treatment of Type 2 diabetes and other conditions.

It’s not a done deal yet, and the board would need to officially approve the upper payment limit in a future board meeting. But the decision signals strong interest in implementing upper payment limits, which would be the board’s first official action to bring down drug costs since it was formed by 2019 legislation.

State board determines two Type 2 diabetes drugs may be unaffordable

The PDAB determined in July that Jardiance and Farxiga were too expensive for Marylanders and could be subject to payment limits.

The board’s work comes as health costs are increasing in Maryland and nationally, with state and federal officials looking for ways to rein in rising prescription drug costs.

Under the Biden administration, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services negotiated with drug makers to lower the costs of expensive prescription drugs for those on Medicare. Those “maximum fair price” negotiations included Farxiga and Jardiance.

The Maryland board will take a cue from those negotiations to help set an upper payment limit for the two drugs purchased on the state’s health insurance plan.

In setting upper payment limits, the board has several metrics that could help set the ceiling on how much the state is willing to spend on the drugs. The board’s staff determined that modeling the upper payment limit on the maximum fair price negotiations will yield the most savings for Maryland.

For Farxiga, the maximum fair price per unit is $5.95, or $178.50 for a 30-day supply. For Jardiance, it’s $6.57 per unit, or $197 for a 30-day supply.

PDAB staff estimates that setting an upper payment limit based on the maximum fair price for Farxiga would save state and local governments an estimated $4.9 million. That estimate does not reflect any rebates or discounts that the state receives for Farxiga, so true savings are not yet clear.

For Jardiance, staff estimates savings could reach $8 million if the state sets an upper payment limit based on maximum fair price. That number, also, does not consider rebates or discounts that the state receives.

But some health advocates fear that upper payment limits will lead to adverse and unintended consequences. Pharmaceutical industry representatioves are also largely against upper payment limits and PDABs in general, arguing that neither is likely to result in lower out-of-pocket costs for everyday Marylanders.

Six drugs were selected for “cost review” by the Prescription Drug Affordability Board address several conditions, including Type 2 diabetes, heart disease, kidney disease, eczema, Crohn’s disease and more.

George Huntley, CEO of Diabetes Patient Advocacy Coalition, asked the board to look at other options in its effort to bring down drug costs.

“Our concern is that UPLs [upper payment limits] will not actually lower the cost for a patient at the pharmacy counter. And our position is we need to lower the cost for the patient at the pharmacy counter and make sure the pharmacy actually stocks the drugs,” he said.

But supporters of the board want swift action, as a new law would allow the board’s authority to expand out to set upper payment limits on the commercial market, not just for state and local purchases. The board will only gain that authority a year after it has successfully implemented upper payment limits on two drugs.

Created by the General Assembly in 2019, the PDAB was slow to launch due in part to a veto from then-Gov. Larry Hogan (R) amid pandemic-induced economic uncertainty in 2020 that delayed the board’s formation.

After Gov. Wes Moore (D) allocated funding for the board’s operation in 2023, the entity went through lengthy rule-making to create the “cost review” process for targeted drugs.

The board finally picked its first six drugs for cost review in May 2024, starting first with Jardiance and Farxiga. On Monday, it added Ozempic and Trulicity for future cost-saving efforts.

Trulicity, the brand name for dulaglutide, is largely used to treat Type 2 diabetes. Ozempic, the brand name for semaglutide, was also developed for Type 2 diabetes, but has recently gained popularity as a weight-loss drug.

Maryland was the first state to create a board for prescription drug cost reduction, with its 2019 legislation, but other states have gotten ahead in the time Maryland’s board was trying to get off the ground.

In October, Colorado’s Prescription Drug Affordability Review Board set the nation’s first upper payment limit on a drug called Enbrel to treat various autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis.
